posts.content_md:
Ok, so this is just an idea or perhaps the beginnings of one. how does TEA function? How fast does it penetrate? Could one differentially expand gelatin by giving a plate a quick rinse in a strong TEA solution, say 10%? Then the resulting bragg planes might just be different making for a more broadband replay.

Any ideas?

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** Ok, so this is just an idea or perhaps the beginnings of one. how does TEA function? How fast does it penetrate? Could one differentially expand gelatin by giving a plate a quick rinse in a strong TEA solution, say 10%? Then the resulting bragg planes might just be different making for a more broadband replay.Any ideas?

Maybe I am wrong but with regards to gelatin swelling, I guess TEA basically

behaves like glycerol. First and foremost the swelling of the layer is

caused by incorporating water. TEA, glycerol, glycols etc. form a

very strong binding with water. I believe with glycerol e.g. it takes

some 250°C or so to get rid of the water. In other words, at the end of the

pre-swelling step (when the layer has been dried), the layer not only

contains TEA but also a significant amount of water.

Higher concentrated glycerol/water mixtures (say at 1:1 ratio) may take an eternity to stabilize a silver halide emulsion. Agfa and Ilford emulsions

treated with such mixtures (never tried that on PFG emulsions) used to

reveal a rather strange behavior: they seemed to have two different levels of swellling, leading thus to the recording of two gratings simultaneously. So one might have got both a red and a blue image on the same emulsion.

I don't know what actually causes this strange swelling behavior - maybe it relates to the "history" of the gelatin layer, to things like hardening etc.

Maybe it's linked to the specific architecture of the emulsion hence

subbing layers etc.would play an important role.

The question of broadband replay we may have to consider along those two basic paths:

- the thickness of the recording material - the thinner the recording layer,

the broader the bandwidth;

- bandwidth of the recording light source. That's where Lippmann photography is paramount.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
I just posted on the thread on PFG-03C that I found an achromat reflection hologram while playing with 03C. I'm guessing that the emulsion was soft enough to have expanded significantly. Normally, you can't get broadband in silver because it's some 200 times harder than DCG. It's the differential swelling in DCG that causes broadband. In silver, it's too hard to differentially swell. However, 03C seems soft enough. This has possibilities for the kind of "colour" that I believe colour holography needs - muted, desaturated colours.

In this vein, is it possible to soften silver halide post exposure, pre-development?

As Martin pointed the key here is not make a very thin holographic emulsion?

Without losing the deep range, the colours may appear very de saturated, if you attain the required refraction index or with sufficient "ni" parameter broadband reflection holograms are possible, however, the emulsion must be as hard as possible because few holographic fringes are available to record all holographic info and development may distort them.

posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** In this vein, is it possible to soften silver halide post exposure, pre-development?

That may depend on the gelatin's "history", e.g. the nature of hardening it

had previously been subjected to.

Since the term "hardening" is far from clear cut, it's not always obvious

what it's referring to.

With the term "softening" things may not get easier. Generally speaking and at least with regards to Agfa's 8E75, hot water, high

pH, hydroxy peroxide, a couple of enzymes were said to "soften" a gelatin emulsion.

> Normally, you can't get broadband in silver because it's some 200 times harder than DCG.

I am aware of certain cases where broadband replay occured on commercial silver halide emulsions - though this is definitely not common pratice:

1) very thin emulsions as already pointed out;

2) SHSG (for certain processing schedules);

3) physical/colloidal development;

4) emulsions recorded in immersion liquids, namely mixtures of

alcohol/water.

> It's the differential swelling in DCG that causes broadband.

Not sure about that. Would be interesting to compare different dichromated colloids with respect to bandwidth. E.g. how does a layer of DC-PVA compare with DCG?

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:5c9bfe9b22]What is HSB?[/quote:5c9bfe9b22]

It's a different color space. It's usually called HSV("Hue", "Saturation", "Value"), but Photoshop uses HSB, substituting V for B ("Brightness").

Color is usually specified, and/or broken down, in terms of a coordinate system. This is because it can then be codified for computer graphic applications, amongst others. Usually, most people use either RGB or CMYK, the former for additive colors such as TV and the latter for printing because ink on paper is a subtractive color process. However, if you want to describe a color in terms of other constituents, you may choose a different set of coordinates more appropriate to your application. Artists, for example, may not care exactly what the RGB or CMYK components are so much as hue and brightness. They would then use a color space where the coords are these values ( [http://developer.apple.com/documentatio ... CI-48.html](http://developer.apple.com/documentation/mac/ACI/ACI-48.html) )

In my case, I'm more intersted in describing the colors of a color hologram in HSV because I think this space is more attuned to the eye as an intuitive representation of real color on a real object. I'm sort of vaguely trying to grasp what "color holography" actually means. Certainly you can always get a "color hologram" simply by using two or three colors on a panchromatic emulsion. But, in display holography, the word "color" in an "artistic" or display sense is not stressed as much as the RGB components, ie the gamut. I'm trying to somehow draw the viewer into the hologram, rather than have it stand as some abstract thing. The colors of a color hologram have mosly seemed "wrong", like early color TV's, except for some of Hans' work I think that a four color gamut is a step in the right direction, but I also think we're focusing on the wrong color coordinate system.

[quote:5c9bfe9b22]Not sure about that. Would be interesting to compare different dichromated colloids with respect to bandwidth. E.g. how does a layer of DC-PVA compare with DCG?[/quote:5c9bfe9b22]

True. Or Nadya's work with glycerin. Michele Boulte gave a talk on PVA this year at SPIE. I tried to get her to talk of the holographic properties but she maintained that the research was in aid of water resistance and that was the focus of her paper.
